terms.meaning: A thing we use to do a job that our bare hands do slowly or cannot do.
terms.example: A spoon stirs the dal. Scissors cut paper. A peeler takes the skin off a potato.
terms.art: A child holding a spoon, a peeler and scissors in a row.

terms.meaning: The thin line where two sides of a thing meet.
terms.example: The edge of a ruler is the thin side. The edge of a paper can cut a finger.
terms.art: A steel ruler seen from the end, with its thin edge marked.

terms.meaning: The flat, thin part of a tool that is made to cut.
terms.example: A knife has a blade. A pair of scissors has two blades.
terms.art: A kitchen knife with its blade coloured and its handle left plain.

terms.meaning: The part of a tool that your hand holds.
terms.example: A knife has a handle. A pan has a handle. A door has a handle.
terms.art: A hand holding the handle of a ladle.

terms.meaning: Having a very thin edge or point that cuts or pricks easily.
terms.example: A new pencil tip is sharp. A broken glass is sharp. A thorn is sharp.
terms.art: A pencil tip, a thorn and a needle side by side.

terms.meaning: Not sharp. The edge or point is thick or worn, so it cuts badly.
terms.example: A butter knife is blunt. A pencil worn down to a stub is blunt.
terms.art: A sharp pencil beside a worn-down pencil stub.

terms.meaning: How hard a push presses on each small bit of a surface. The same push on a smaller place gives more pressure.
terms.example: Your finger pushes gently on your hand. A pencil tip with the same push hurts, because the tip is tiny.
terms.art: A finger and a pencil tip pressing on a hand, with the same arrow.

terms.meaning: A curved blade fixed upright on a wooden board. The cook holds the board still with a foot and moves the food against the blade.
terms.example: Many kitchens in Tamil Nadu and Kerala have an aruvamanai for cutting brinjal and pumpkin. In Bengal the same tool is a boti.
terms.art: A cook sitting on the floor with a foot on a board and a curved blade standing up.

terms.meaning: The soft, stretchy cover over your whole body.
terms.example: Skin keeps water and blood in, and dust and germs out.
terms.art: A child's arm with the top layer of skin shown in cross-section.

terms.meaning: A place where the skin has been opened along a line.
terms.example: A paper can give a cut on your finger. A cut can bleed.
terms.art: A fingertip with a thin red line on it.

terms.meaning: Living beings too small to see. Some of them can make you ill.
terms.example: Germs can sit on a dirty knife or on soil. Washing with clean water carries them away.
terms.art: A tiny dot-like group of germs on a fingertip, drawn very large.

terms.meaning: Tiny sensors in your skin. They send messages to your brain about touch, heat and pain.
terms.example: Your fingertips have very many nerve endings. That is why a paper cut stings so much.
terms.art: A finger with tiny threads running from the skin to a line going up the arm.

terms.meaning: The feeling that tells you something is hurt or in danger.
terms.example: You touch a hot pan and feel pain. It tells you to pull your hand away.
terms.art: A hand pulling away from a hot pan with a small alarm bell drawn above it.

terms.meaning: Tiny pieces of cells that float in your blood. They stick together to close a cut.
terms.example: One drop of blood has millions of platelets. When you cut yourself, they rush to the cut.
terms.art: A drop of blood with small round platelets sticking together at a gap.

terms.meaning: A plug made of platelets and thin threads that stops blood from flowing out.
terms.example: A small cut bleeds, and then a clot forms and the bleeding stops.
terms.art: A cut with a small dark plug closing it.

terms.meaning: The dry, hard cover that a clot makes over a cut while new skin grows underneath.
terms.example: A scab itches when new skin is growing. It falls off when the skin is ready.
terms.art: A knee with a brown scab on it.

terms.meaning: The first help we give to someone who is hurt, before a doctor is needed or comes.
terms.example: Pressing a clean cloth on a cut is first aid. So is cooling a burn under a tap.
terms.art: A child pressing a clean cloth on a friend's finger.

terms.meaning: A small sticky cover that goes over a cut to keep it clean.
terms.example: After you wash a small cut, a plaster keeps dust and germs away.
terms.art: A finger with a plaster wrapped around it.

terms.meaning: A kind of living being, too small to see. Some bacteria make us ill. Many are helpful.
terms.example: Curd is made with helpful bacteria. Tetanus is made by harmful bacteria in soil.
terms.art: A few round and rod-shaped bacteria, drawn very large, beside a dot of soil.

terms.meaning: A serious illness caused by bacteria that live in soil. They can get in through a deep or dirty cut.
terms.example: A deep cut from a nail that lay in the mud needs a doctor, because of tetanus.
terms.art: A nail lying in mud, with tiny bacteria drawn around the nail.

terms.meaning: Tough, sleeping forms that some bacteria make so they can wait for a long time.
terms.example: Tetanus bacteria wait in soil as spores. They wake up in a deep cut with no air.
terms.art: A soil crumb with tiny sealed seeds inside it.

terms.meaning: The brown flakes that form when iron joins with oxygen from air and water.
terms.example: An old iron nail left in the rain turns rusty. Rust does not cause tetanus.
terms.art: A nail half shiny and half brown with rust.

terms.meaning: What moves from a hotter thing into a cooler thing when they touch.
terms.example: Heat moves from a hot pan into your cooler hand. Heat moves from your hand into an ice cube.
terms.art: A hot pan and a hand with an arrow of heat going from pan to hand.

terms.meaning: The tiny bits that everything is made of. They are far too small to see and they never stop jiggling.
terms.example: In a hot pan the particles jiggle fast. In a cool plate they jiggle slowly.
terms.art: A hot pan and a cool plate, each with a close-up of fast and slow jiggling dots.

terms.meaning: A material that heat moves through quickly.
terms.example: A steel spoon in hot dal gets a hot handle soon. Steel is a conductor.
terms.art: A steel spoon in a pot with arrows of heat running up the handle.

terms.meaning: A material that heat moves through slowly.
terms.example: A wooden spoon stays cool at the top. A thick dry cloth lets you hold a hot pot. Both are insulators.
terms.art: A wooden spoon in a pot with a short arrow of heat that stops low on the handle.

terms.meaning: A burn made by a hot liquid or by steam.
terms.example: A cup of hot tea that spills on skin gives a scald. So does steam from a pot.
terms.art: A cup of tea tipping with drops falling towards a hand.

terms.meaning: The hot gas that rises from boiling water. It is hotter than it looks.
terms.example: Steam comes out of a pressure cooker's whistle. It can burn your hand.
terms.art: A pressure cooker with steam coming from its whistle and a hand held far away.

terms.meaning: A very fast movement that your body makes to protect you, before you have time to think.
terms.example: You touch something hot and your hand jumps away. That is a reflex.
terms.art: A hand jumping back from a hot pan with a line to the spine and back.

terms.meaning: The thick bundle of nerves inside your backbone. It carries messages between your body and your brain.
terms.example: When your hand touches something hot, a message goes up the arm to the spinal cord. The cord sends back 'pull away'.
terms.art: A child's back with the spinal cord drawn as a line inside the backbone.

terms.meaning: Skin that is hurt by heat.
terms.example: Hot oil can give a burn. So can a hot pan or a flame.
terms.art: A hand with a red patch on the back of it.

terms.meaning: A small bubble on the skin, filled with clear liquid. The body makes it to cover a burn.
terms.example: A burn can make a blister. Leave the blister alone. Popping it lets germs in.
terms.art: A fingertip with a small clear bubble.

terms.meaning: Something that can burn, such as cooking gas, oil, wood or cloth.
terms.example: The gas in a cylinder is the fuel for the stove. Wood is the fuel for a fire.
terms.art: A gas cylinder, a log and a lamp with oil, all labelled fuel.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air that fire needs, and that all of us need to breathe.
terms.example: A lid on a burning pan stops the air getting in, so the flame goes out.
terms.art: A pan with a lid pressed on top, and small oxygen dots outside it.

terms.meaning: A flow of tiny charged particles through a wire. It makes a mixer spin and a bulb glow.
terms.example: Electricity runs through the wire of a mixer from the plug to the motor.
terms.art: A plug, a wire and a mixer with small dots flowing along the wire.

terms.meaning: What happens when electricity flows through a body. It can be very dangerous.
terms.example: Touching a plug with wet hands can give an electric shock. A grown-up does the plugging in.
terms.art: A wet hand near a plug with a big red cross over it.

terms.meaning: The pull of the Earth on everything. It pulls things down towards the ground.
terms.example: Let go of a steel tumbler and gravity pulls it down. A dropped tumbler falls to the floor.
terms.art: A tumbler falling from a hand with an arrow pointing down.

terms.meaning: How hard the Earth pulls a thing downwards. A heavier thing has a bigger pull on it.
terms.example: A full water bottle has more weight than an empty one. It pushes down harder on your hand.
terms.art: Two hands, one holding an empty bottle and one a full bottle.

terms.meaning: Anything that you carry or lift.
terms.example: A bag of rice is a load. A school bag with all your books is a load.
terms.art: A child carrying a bag of rice close to the chest.

terms.meaning: The place where all of a thing's weight seems to act. A thing falls when this point moves past the edge of its base.
terms.example: A pencil on its flat end tips with a blow. A pencil lying down stays put.
terms.art: A tall box and a low box each with a dot at the balance point.

terms.meaning: Having more weight high up than low down, so that it tips over easily.
terms.example: A cupboard with heavy things on the top shelf is top-heavy.
terms.art: A tall cupboard with a heavy bag on the top shelf, starting to lean.

terms.meaning: The chance that something will cause harm. It has two parts: how likely the harm is, and how bad it would be.
terms.example: A cut with a plastic knife has a small risk. Lifting a pot of boiling water has a big risk.
terms.art: Two scales, one with a small cut and one with a pot of boiling water.

terms.meaning: A part that opens by itself to let out pressure, so that a pot or a cooker cannot burst.
terms.example: A pressure cooker has a safety valve. If the pressure climbs too high, the valve opens.
terms.art: A pressure cooker with its small valve letting out a puff of steam.

terms.meaning: A phone number to call when someone is badly hurt or in danger. In India it is 112.
terms.example: If a grown-up cannot wake up or a burn is big, call 112. Put the number where everyone can see it.
terms.art: A phone with 112 on the screen and a card with 112 on the fridge door.

experiments.title: Thin edge, thick edge: which goes deepest into dough?
experiments.question: The push is the same. So does a thin edge go deeper into dough than a wide palm?
experiments.predict: Put the five tools in a line. Put the one you think will go deepest first, and the one you think will go least last. Then say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the tool. Use the same slab of dough and the same child pushing. Press as gently as you would press a ripe mango, and count slowly to three. Use a fresh spot each time. Do it 3 times, because one try can be a fluke. Smooth the dough flat between rounds.
results_table: What I saw (dent, line or cut)
Round 1: how deep (shallow, middle or deep)

materials.item: 2 cups of atta and about three-quarters of a cup of water, mixed into a soft dough (it should feel like a soft earlobe)
a steel ruler (a plastic ruler also works, but it cuts a little less deep)
a steel spoon
a thin cotton thread about 40 centimetres long (dental floss also works), with a pencil tied to each end
a flat tray or a big steel plate to work on
a pencil and the results table

experiments.safety: A grown-up sits beside the child for the whole test. No knife is used. Hold the ruler by its flat sides and keep fingers away from its thin edge. The pencils on the thread keep fingers safe.

schedule.what: Make the dough slab. Guess. Test five tools three times. Say what changed.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the five marks the tools left in the dough, side by side, from the widest to the narrowest.
experiments.context: This is the main test of the lesson. You push five tools into soft dough with the same gentle push. You find out what makes some things cut and others only dent.

flow.do: 1. Mix 2 cups of atta with about three-quarters of a cup of water. 2. Knead for 2 minutes, until it is soft and does not stick. Add a pinch of atta if it sticks, or a few drops of water if it crumbles. 3. Pat it into a slab as long as your child's forearm, as wide as a hand and as thick as two fingers.
flow.say: We are going to push five different things into this dough. The dough shows us how deep each push goes.
flow.kid: Help to make the dough slab. It should be soft and as thick as two fingers.
flow.context: This step makes the dough slab for the test. The dough is soft, so it shows even a small difference between the tools.

flow.do: Lay out the five tools: the palm, the flat ruler, the spoon, the ruler's edge and the thread. Ask your child to line them up, deepest first.
flow.say: I will press all five into the dough with the same gentle push. Which will go deepest? Which will go least? Put them in a line and tell me why.
flow.kid: Look at the five tools. Which will go deepest into the dough? Put that one first. Say why.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. It is a guess, and the dough will answer it.

ask.q: Why did you put that one first?
good: It is thin.
It looks like a knife.
It is the hardest.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to press the flat of the left palm into the dough for a count of three. 2. Lay the ruler flat on the dough and press the same way. 3. Look at both marks together.
flow.say: Press as gently as you press a ripe mango. Count one, two, three. What mark do you see?
flow.kid: Press your palm into the dough. Count to three. Look at the mark. Now do the same with the flat ruler.

ask.q: What mark did your palm leave?
good: A wide, shallow dent.
A round dip.
It did not cut.

flow.do: Ask your child to press the back of the spoon into a fresh spot for a count of three. Look at the mark.
flow.say: Now the back of the spoon. Same gentle push. Count to three. What mark is this?
flow.kid: Press the back of the spoon in a fresh spot. Count to three. Look at the mark.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ruler upright on its thin edge, with your fingers on its flat sides. Fold a clean cloth over the top end, so your child presses on soft cloth and not on a thin steel end. 2. Your child lays one palm on the top end and presses the same gentle push for a count of three. 3. Look at the mark.
flow.say: Now the thin edge. We use the same gentle push. Look at how far it goes in.
flow.kid: A grown-up holds the ruler on its thin edge. Press down gently on the cloth on top, to a count of three. Look at the mark.
flow.parent: If the edge only makes a narrow groove, that is the right result. It still goes far deeper than the palm.

ask.q: How is this mark different from the palm mark?
good: It is thin and deep.
It went in much further.
It made a line.

flow.do: 1. Wind each end of the thread round a pencil, so the pencils are the handles. 2. Pull the thread tight and lay it across the slab. 3. Press straight down with both hands, gently, and keep pressing until the thread reaches the tray.
flow.say: Now the thinnest thing of all, a thread. Hold it tight and press it down gently. What happens?
flow.kid: A grown-up helps. Wind the thread on two pencils and pull it tight. Press it down slowly through the dough.
flow.context: This is the last of the five tools. A tight thread is much thinner than the edge of a ruler.
flow.parent: A tight cotton thread goes right through soft dough, like the wire in a cheese cutter. If it does not, pull it tighter or check the dough is soft.

flow.do: Smooth the dough flat. Do the palm, flat ruler, spoon, ruler edge and thread again, in the same order, with the same gentle push. Then do it a third time. Write the depths in the table.
flow.say: We try everything again, two more times. One try can be a fluke, but three tries together are more trustworthy.
flow.kid: Smooth the dough. Try all five again. Then try them once more. Write what you see.

flow.do: Look at all the marks. Ask your child to put the five tools in a line again, deepest first. Compare with the first guess.
flow.say: Look at the marks. Which tool went deepest? Which went least? The push was the same every time. So what was different?
flow.kid: Look at the marks. Which tool went deepest? The push was the same. What was different?
flow.parent: This test shows that a smaller place gives a deeper cut. It cannot tell us whether a sharp knife or a blunt knife hurts more people. People still disagree about that.

ask.q: What changed from tool to tool?
good: The size of the part that touched the dough.
Thin tools went deeper.
The thread touched the dough in a thin line.

check.q: The push was the same. Why did the thread cut the dough and the palm did not?
options: The thread is made of steel.
The thread pushes harder than a palm.
The thread touches a much smaller place, so the push is bigger there.
check.why: The push stayed the same. A palm is wide, so its push spreads out. A thread is thin, so the whole push lands on a tiny line. Picking 'pushes harder' mixes up the push with the place it lands on.

experiments.title: Steel or wood: which feels colder, and which melts an ice cube faster?
experiments.question: Steel and wood have been in the same room all day. Why does steel feel colder?
experiments.predict: Guess which will feel colder, the steel plate or the wooden board. Then guess which will melt an ice cube faster. Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the material. Put the steel plate and the wooden board side by side in the same room. Use two ice cubes of the same size. Put them down at the same moment. Look at the same times. If you can, do the whole test twice.
results_table: Ice on steel: water around it (none, a little, a lot)
Ice on wood: water around it (none, a little, a lot)

materials.item: a steel plate or a steel thali
a wooden chopping board, tray or plank about the same size (a thick cardboard works too)
2 ice cubes of the same size, from the freezer
a clock or a phone timer
a paper towel for wiping up water

schedule.what: Guess. Touch both plates. Put an ice cube on each. Look every 2 minutes for 8 minutes. Say what you found.

experiments.record: Write 'steel' or 'wood' for each: Which felt colder? Which had more water after 8 minutes? Draw the two plates with their ice cubes and the water around them.
experiments.context: Heat moves into cooler things. In this test you feel how fast heat leaves your hand through steel and through wood, and you watch it melt ice.

flow.do: 1. Leave the steel plate and the wooden board side by side on a table for 10 minutes. Then both are the room's warmth. 2. Ask your child to guess which will feel colder when touched. 3. Ask which will melt ice faster.
flow.say: Both have been in this room all day. Which one do you think will feel colder? Which will melt ice faster? Tell me why.
flow.kid: Look at the steel plate and the wooden board. Which will feel colder? Which will melt ice faster? Say why.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Both are the same warmth as the room.

ask.q: Why do you think that one will be colder?
good: Steel is cold metal.
Wood is warm.
I have felt steel feel cold.

flow.do: Ask your child to lay one palm flat on the steel and one on the wood, for a slow count of five. Then swap hands.
flow.say: Put one hand on each. Count to five slowly. Which one feels colder? Swap your hands. Does it still feel the same?
flow.kid: Put your palm on the steel. Count to five. Put your other palm on the wood. Which feels colder? Swap hands.
flow.parent: Both are as warm as the room, so a thermometer would show the same number for both. Steel feels colder because heat leaves your hand through steel much faster.

ask.q: Which felt colder, and did it change when you swapped hands?
good: The steel felt colder both times.
It was the plate, not my hand.

flow.do: Put one ice cube on the steel plate and one on the wooden board, at the same moment. Note the time.
flow.say: Put both ice cubes down together. Now we watch.
flow.kid: Put one ice cube on the steel. Put one on the wood. Do it at the same moment.

flow.do: Look at the two ice cubes every 2 minutes, four times. Each time, write 'none', 'a little' or 'a lot' for the water around each cube. Wipe the plate dry if you test again.
flow.say: Look at both ice cubes. Which has more water around it now? Write it down.
flow.kid: Look every 2 minutes. Which ice cube has more water around it? Write it down.
flow.parent: If the ice has not melted at all after 8 minutes, use a smaller cube or wait 4 more minutes. In winter, the steel plate still wins. No ice at all? The touch test in steps 1 and 2 is the whole test.

ask.q: What do you see at the 4-minute look?
good: More water under the ice on the steel.
The ice on the steel is smaller.

flow.do: Compare the two plates. Ask your child to say which melted the ice faster and how that matches the touch test.
flow.say: Which ice cube melted faster? What does that tell you about steel? Why did the steel feel colder to your hand?
flow.kid: Which ice cube melted faster? Why did steel feel colder to your hand?
flow.parent: Science cannot tell us how a feeling of 'cold' arises. We can only say what the sensors in the skin respond to. This test cannot show how hot things move heat into skin, but it is the same idea in the other direction.

ask.q: Why did the ice melt faster on the steel?
good: Heat from the room moved into the ice through the steel faster.
Steel lets heat go through quickly.

check.q: The two plates are the same warmth. Why does steel feel colder?
options: The steel is colder than the wood.
Heat leaves your hand through steel faster than through wood.
check.why: Heat moves from your warmer hand into the plate. Steel lets heat through quickly, so your hand loses heat fast and feels cold. Wood lets heat through slowly. Picking 'steel is colder' is what it feels like, but a thermometer shows both are the same.

activities.title: Working part, holding part: a tool tour of the kitchen

materials.item: a paper and a pencil
6 small paper arrows, or sticky notes

schedule.what: Walk through the kitchen with a grown-up and find the working part and the holding part of six tools.

activities.record: Draw one tool. Colour the working part red and the holding part green.
activities.context: Each tool you use has two parts. This tour helps you find both on tools in your own kitchen.

flow.do: Explain the tour. Remind your child that the hand goes only on the holding part.
flow.say: Every tool has a working part and a holding part. The working part does the job. The holding part is where your hand goes. Let us find six.
flow.kid: Every tool has a working part and a holding part. Your hand goes only on the holding part. Let us find six tools.

flow.do: Walk through the kitchen with your child. Look at a spoon, a peeler, a grater, a ladle, round-tip scissors and the knob of the gas stove. For each one, your child points with a pencil at the working part. Your child then puts a paper arrow on the holding part. A grown-up picks up anything with an edge. The stove stays off.
flow.say: Point at the working part with your pencil, from far away. Now put an arrow on the holding part. What does the tool do? Where does your hand go?
flow.kid: Point at the working part with a pencil. Do not touch it. Put an arrow on the holding part. Say what the tool does.
flow.parent: Good finds: a peeler's blade hides in a slot. A grater's holes do the work. A ladle's wooden handle stays cool. A stove's knob is the only part a hand touches.

flow.do: Sit together and look at the arrows. Ask which tool had a guard that kept the working part away from the hand.
flow.say: Which tool kept its working part furthest from your hand? Which tool would you change, to make it safer?
flow.kid: Which tool keeps its working part far from your hand? Which one would you change?

ask.q: Which tool keeps your hand furthest from the working part?
good: The peeler.
The grater, because I hold the frame.
The ladle.

activities.title: Carry it, pass it, let it fall: practice with pretend tools

materials.item: a wooden spoon and a ruler, as pretend knives
a pair of round-tip school scissors (closed) with paper to cut
a banana

activities.safety: A grown-up stays beside the child. The practice uses a wooden spoon and a ruler as pretend knives. No real knife is used.

schedule.what: Practice three safe habits: where the edge points, where the fingers go, where the eyes look.

activities.record: Draw yourself carrying scissors safely. Show which way the points face.
activities.context: A safe cut needs three habits: the edge points away, the fingers stay out of its way, and the eyes watch it. You practise with pretend tools.

flow.do: Show the cat's-paw hold. Curl the fingertips of the holding hand under, so the knuckles face the pretend knife. Ask your child to hold a banana with a cat's-paw hand. Then they slide the wooden spoon along the banana without pressing.
flow.say: Curl your fingertips under, like a cat's paw. Now your knuckles are near the knife and your fingertips are safe. Slide the wooden spoon, with the edge away from you.
flow.kid: Curl your fingertips under like a cat's paw. Hold the banana. Slide the wooden spoon along the banana, away from your body.

flow.do: Show how to carry closed scissors: hold them closed by the rings, points down and close to your leg, and walk. Then ask your child to carry the ruler, edge down, beside the leg, across the room and back. Walk, do not run.
flow.say: To carry a tool with an edge, hold it close, point it down, and walk slowly. Never run.
flow.kid: Carry the closed scissors by the rings, points down. Walk slowly across the room. Then carry the ruler the same way.

flow.do: Pass the pretend knife. The giver lays the ruler on the table. The other person picks it up by the holding end. Take turns. Then do the same with the closed scissors.
flow.say: To pass a tool, lay it on the table. The other person picks it up. Nothing goes from hand to hand.
flow.kid: Lay the ruler on the table for your grown-up. They pick it up by the handle end. Then swap.

flow.do: Drop the wooden spoon on the floor, on purpose. Ask your child to step back, away from it, and not to catch it. Then practise 'put it down first': hold the ruler, then call your child's name. Your child puts it down on the table, then looks up.
flow.say: A falling tool has no handle in the air. Step back and let it fall. If someone calls you, put the tool down first, then look up.
flow.kid: A grown-up drops the spoon. Step back and let it fall. Next, they call your name. Put your tool down first. Then look up.

ask.q: Why do we put the tool down before we look up?
good: My hand might move when my eyes move.
I should watch the edge all the time.

setup.caption: 1. Curl your fingertips like a cat's paw.

setup.caption: 2. Carry the tool close, points down, and walk.

activities.think: Which of the three habits do you think is the easiest to forget? How could you remember it?

activities.title: Teddy needs first aid: a cut and a burn

materials.item: a toy or doll that can get a little wet
2 small stickers or paper dots, one red for a cut and one orange for a burn
a clean cloth
a plaster or a strip of cloth with tape
a mug of water and a bowl
a clock or a phone timer

schedule.what: Practise first aid on a toy: press, wash and cover a cut, then cool a burn.

activities.record: Draw the three steps for a cut and the three for a burn on a folded sheet.
activities.context: You learn first aid for a cut and for a burn by practising on a toy. When you have practised, you know what to do on the day.

flow.do: Put a red sticker on the toy's paw as a cut and an orange sticker on its other paw as a burn. Say these are pretend.
flow.say: Teddy has a cut on one paw and a burn on the other. We are going to help. What is the very first thing to do? Tell a grown-up.
flow.kid: Teddy has a pretend cut and a pretend burn. First, tell a grown-up. We will help Teddy.

flow.do: 1. Press the clean cloth firmly on the red sticker. 2. Count slowly to 30. Say that a real cut needs five minutes, and the cloth is not lifted to peep. 3. Hold up the paw, higher than the heart.
flow.say: Press the clean cloth on the cut. Do not lift it to peep. For a real cut, we press for five minutes. Hold the paw up high.
flow.kid: Press the clean cloth on the red dot. Count to 30. A real cut needs five minutes. Do not peep.

flow.do: 1. Pour a little water from the mug over the red sticker, so it runs off into the bowl. 2. Dab the paw dry with a clean cloth. 3. Cover the paw with a plaster or a strip of cloth.
flow.say: Now we wash. Clean running water carries dirt and germs away. Then we cover with a clean plaster.
flow.kid: Pour clean water over the cut. Dab it dry. Cover it with a plaster.

flow.do: 1. Move to the orange sticker. Say: tell a grown-up, then cool it. 2. Pour cool water slowly over the burn from the mug, again and again, for one minute. Say that a real burn needs about 20 minutes. 3. Cover it loosely with a clean cloth.
flow.say: A burn keeps burning after you pull away. We take the heat out with cool running water. A real burn needs about 20 minutes. No ice, no ghee, no toothpaste.
flow.kid: Pour cool water over the burn for one minute. A real burn needs 20 minutes. Cover it with a clean cloth. No ice, ghee or toothpaste.

ask.q: Why do we use cool running water and not ice?
good: Ice can harm the skin again.
Water carries the heat away.

flow.do: Read out when a doctor is needed. Blood still flows after ten minutes of pressing. The cut is deep, gaping or dirty. A bite from an animal needs a doctor too. So does a cut on the face. A burn is bigger than a palm, has blisters, or is on the face or hands. Ask your child to say one of them back.
flow.say: Some hurts need a doctor. A cut that keeps bleeding, a deep or dirty cut, or a burn bigger than your palm. Can you say one?
flow.kid: Some hurts need a doctor. Can you name one? A burn bigger than your palm is one.

options: A tiny scratch that stopped bleeding.
A small cut that a plaster now covers.
A deep cut from a nail that lay in the mud.
check.why: A deep, dirty cut can let tetanus bacteria in, so a doctor is needed. A small scratch that has stopped bleeding can be washed and covered at home. Picking the plaster option means thinking every cut needs a doctor.

setup.caption: 1. Teddy has a pretend cut and a pretend burn.

setup.art: A child pressing a clean cloth on teddy's paw, then pouring water over it.
setup.caption: 2. Press the cut. Then wash it. Then cover it.

setup.caption: 3. Cool the burn under water. A real burn takes about 20 minutes.

activities.think: Why do you think cooling needs so long? What is the water doing to the heat in the skin?
activities.problem: What do you do first, and next, for a cut and for a burn?

activities.title: Close or far: how a bottle feels at your chest and at arm's length

materials.item: a 1-litre water bottle, full
a 1-kilogram bag of rice or lentils, or a bag with a few books
a clock with a seconds hand, or a phone timer

schedule.what: Hold the bottle close and far. Lift the bag with bent knees.

activities.record: Write how many seconds you held the bottle close and how many seconds you held it far.
activities.context: A load feels heavier the farther it is from your body. You test this, and then learn the leg way to lift.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to hold the full bottle against their chest with both arms. Count seconds until the arms say 'I am tired', or stop at 30. 2. Rest. 3. Ask them to hold the same bottle with straight arms in front. Count seconds again.
flow.say: Hold the bottle close to your chest. Count the seconds until you feel tired. Now hold it out in front with straight arms. Count again. Which is harder? Why?
flow.kid: Hold the bottle against your chest. Count the seconds. Now hold it out in front. Count again. Which is harder?
flow.parent: Stop sooner if the arms shake. The bottle weighs the same both times. The farther a load is from the body, the harder the muscles work.

ask.q: The bottle is the same. Why did it get harder?
good: It was far from my body.
My arm had to work harder.
My shoulder was doing more.

flow.do: 1. Put the bag of rice on the floor. 2. Show how to stand close, feet apart, bend the knees, hug the bag to the chest, and stand up using the legs. 3. Let your child do the same. First tip one corner of the bag to feel if it is too heavy.
flow.say: Stand close to the bag. Bend your knees, not your back. Hug the bag to your chest. Stand up using your legs. Tip a corner first to check it is not too heavy.
flow.kid: Stand close to the bag. Bend your knees. Hug the bag. Stand up with your legs.

flow.do: Ask your child to say when a thing is too heavy to lift alone and what to do instead.
flow.say: If a thing is too heavy, what do we do? We can share it, slide it, roll it or leave it for a grown-up.
flow.kid: If a bag is too heavy, what can you do? Share it, slide it, roll it, or ask a grown-up.

setup.caption: 1. Hold the bottle close. Count the seconds.

setup.art: A child holding the same bottle with straight arms in front, arms shaking a little.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the bottle far away. Count again.

setup.caption: 3. Bend your knees and hug the bag.

activities.problem: How does the distance from your body change how hard a load is to hold?

activities.title: Top-heavy box: where should the heavy bag go?

materials.item: a tall empty cardboard box such as a cereal box, with its top flaps closed
a small bag of rice or lentils, about as heavy as a water bottle
masking tape or sticky tape
paper and pencil

schedule.what: Test the box empty, with the heavy bag at the bottom, and with the heavy bag at the top.

activities.record: Fill in: Empty, bag at the bottom, bag at the top. For each, write the level of poke that tipped the box: touch, tap, firm push, or it did not fall.
activities.context: A thing with its weight high up tips over easily. In this activity you tip a box three ways to find where the heavy part belongs.

flow.do: Stand the empty box on its small end on a table. Ask your child to guess where the heavy bag should go to make the box hardest to tip over. Write the guess.
flow.say: Where should the heavy bag go to make the box hardest to tip over: at the bottom, at the top, or in the middle? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Where should the heavy bag go to make the box hardest to tip over? Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think that is the place?
good: Heavy things stay down.
At the bottom it is more steady.

flow.do: 1. Test the empty box. Poke the top edge sideways with one finger. Try a touch, then a tap, then a firm push. Write the first level that tips it. 2. Open the top flap, push the bag to the bottom, close the flap, and stand the box up. 3. Poke the same way. Write the level that tips it.
flow.say: First poke the empty box at the top. Touch, tap, then a firm push. When does it fall? Now put the bag at the bottom. Poke the same way.
flow.kid: Poke the empty box at the top. Touch, then tap, then a firm push. Write when it falls. Now put the bag at the bottom. Poke again.

flow.do: 1. Take the bag out. Tape it inside the box near the top. 2. Stand the box up and poke the same way. Write the level that tips it. 3. Do each of the three tests twice, in the same order, to check.
flow.say: Now tape the bag near the top. Poke the same way. What happens? Check each test twice.
flow.kid: Tape the bag near the top. Poke the same way. Does it fall sooner or later? Check twice.

flow.do: Compare the three results. Ask your child why a cupboard with heavy things on top is dangerous. Ask where heavy things should go.
flow.say: Which way was the hardest to tip? Why? Where should the heavy things go on a shelf?
flow.kid: Which way was the hardest to tip? Where should heavy things go on a shelf?
flow.parent: With the bag at the bottom the box usually needs a firm push or does not fall. With the bag at the top a touch can tip it. If the box is too short to tip at all, use a taller box.

ask.q: Where should the heavy things go on a shelf, and why?
good: On the bottom shelf, so the cupboard is steady.
Low, so it will not tip.

activities.title: A cold-kitchen safety check, with everything off

materials.item: paper and a pencil for the check list

activities.safety: A grown-up first turns off everything and checks that the stove, the pans and the iron are cold. The child touches nothing hot. If anything was in use in the last hour, do this check later.

schedule.what: Walk through the kitchen and tick off eight safety checks. Choose one thing to change.

activities.record: Write the eight checks and tick each one. Write one thing you want to change.
activities.context: Most injuries to young children happen at home, and the kitchen is a common place. You check your own kitchen with a grown-up when everything is off and cold.

flow.do: Turn off the gas at the knob and at the cylinder or main gas tap. Check that the pans and the stove are cold. Unplug the mixer, the kettle and the iron, pulling by the plug. Say what you have done.
flow.say: First, we make everything safe. The gas is off. Everything is cold. The mixer is unplugged.
flow.kid: A grown-up makes everything safe first. The gas is off and everything is cold.

flow.do: Walk through the kitchen with your child. Look at eight things and tick each one. 1. Are the pan handles turned inwards? 2. Is a long dupatta, loose sleeve or long hair tied back? 3. Are the knives and scissors put away, not left in a sink of soapy water? 4. Is anything heavy on a high shelf? 5. Are the plugs and wires whole, with no bare copper showing? 6. Is a tall cupboard or a television steady? 7. Is the emergency number 112 on view? 8. Is there a clean cloth and a plaster near?
flow.say: Let us check eight things. For each one, you say yes or no, and we tick it.
flow.kid: Walk with a grown-up. Look at eight things. Say yes or no for each, and tick it.
flow.parent: Let your child lead. Where an answer is no, do not fix it yet. Step 3 is for choosing what to change.

flow.do: Ask your child to choose the one check that matters most and to say what could happen if it were a no. Make the change together or write it on the project map.
flow.say: Which of the eight matters most in our kitchen? What could go wrong if it were a no? What shall we change first?
flow.kid: Which of the eight matters most? What could go wrong? What will you change first?

ask.q: Which check matters most in our kitchen, and why?
good: Heavy things low, because they could fall.
Pan handles in, because someone could knock one.

setup.caption: 1. Everything is off and cold. Look at the eight places.

projects.title: Our Safe-Home Map and the 112 card

materials.item: a big sheet of paper, or two sheets taped together
3 colours: green, orange and red
a card or paper for the emergency card, and tape
a pencil and a ruler

projects.safety: A grown-up moves heavy things and anything that has been near heat. The child draws and decides.

schedule.what: Draw a map of the kitchen. Colour eight places green, orange or red.
Make one change together. Write the 112 card and put it where everyone can see it.
Tell a family member one rule from the map. Look again and add one thing.

projects.record: Keep the map. Write the one change you made, and where the 112 card is.
projects.context: In this project you draw your own kitchen. You mark the places that are safe for you, the places for a grown-up beside you, and the grown-up's jobs. Then you make one real change.

flow.do: Walk through the kitchen with your child and look at the places where something sharp, hot or heavy is kept or used. Ask what they notice.
flow.say: Let us look at our kitchen like safety detectives. Where do we keep or use something sharp? Where is something hot? Where is something heavy?
flow.kid: Walk through the kitchen. Where is something sharp, hot or heavy? Find eight places.

flow.do: Help your child to draw a map of the kitchen, as if looking down from the ceiling. Mark eight places. Colour each green (I can do it alone), orange (with a grown-up beside me) or red (a grown-up's job).
flow.say: Draw our kitchen from above. Put in the stove, the sink, the shelf and the cupboard. Colour eight places. Green means I can do it alone. Orange means a grown-up is beside me. Red means it is a grown-up's job.
flow.kid: Draw the kitchen from above. Mark eight places. Colour each one green, orange or red.
flow.parent: Do not argue about the colours. If your child puts the stove green, ask: 'What could happen?' and let them change it.

flow.do: Choose one change from the map, together. For example: move a heavy bag to a low shelf, turn the pan handles inwards, or tie the dupatta back. A grown-up does anything heavy. Make the change.
flow.say: Which one change would make our kitchen safer? Let us make it now.
flow.kid: Choose one change. A grown-up helps you make it. Now look at the map again.

ask.q: Which one change matters most, and why?
good: Heavy things low, so they cannot fall on us.
Pan handles in, so nobody knocks them.

flow.do: Write 112 big on a card. Write 'Emergency: 112' and the family's address and one phone number a child can read out. Tape the card where everyone can see it, such as the fridge door.
flow.say: In India, 112 is the number to call for any emergency. Let us write it big and put it where everybody can see it.
flow.kid: Write 112 big on a card. Add your address. Tape it on the fridge door.
flow.parent: Say that 112 is for when someone is badly hurt, will not wake up, or a fire starts. It is never for play. Practise saying the address aloud together.

flow.do: A day or two later, ask your child to tell another family member one rule from the map. Look at the map again and add one more thing you have noticed.
flow.say: Tell someone one rule from your map. What have you noticed since? Add it to the map.
flow.kid: Tell someone at home one rule from your map. Add one new thing you noticed.

challenges.title: A cover for a pretend blade
challenges.problem: Make a cover for a pretend blade, so that it can be carried and put in a drawer and nobody can touch its edge.
constraints: The pretend blade is a strip of stiff card about 3 centimetres wide and 20 centimetres long. Tape it to a ruler or wooden spoon as the handle.
The cover must not let the strip touch your skin, even when you shake the cover three times.
You may use card, paper and tape. A grown-up does any cutting.
materials: a strip of stiff card from a box
a ruler or wooden spoon for a handle
general: Fold a card in half and tape the sides to make a sleeve. The blade slides in and out, like a pencil in a case.
Make a box with a slot, like a block that holds knives. The blade slides into the slot, handle up.
Add a guard: a flat card across the handle that stops the hand sliding up onto the blade.
creative: Make a sheath that hangs on a hook, so the blade points down and the handle is easy to reach.
Make a cover that closes by itself when you let go, with a folded card that springs shut.
Make a wall holder high up on the wall, with a magnet strip, as some kitchens do.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own way to keep a blade safe. Test it with three shakes. Then ask a friend to find a weakness. There is more than one good answer.

flow.do: Help your child make the pretend blade. A grown-up cuts the card strip. Tape the strip to the ruler for a handle.
flow.say: Here is our pretend blade. It cannot cut anything, but we will treat it as if it could. The job is to design a cover that keeps everyone safe.
flow.kid: Make a pretend blade from a card strip taped to a ruler. A grown-up cuts the card.
flow.context: This is the first step of the cover challenge. You make a pretend blade, so that you can practise safety design without any real danger.

flow.do: Ask your child to think of three ideas for covering the blade before trying any. Ask them to say which of their ideas takes the danger away and which only hides it.
flow.say: Engineers ask three questions. Can we take the danger away? Can we put a guard in the way? What must the person remember? Let us think of three ideas.
flow.kid: Say three ideas for covering the blade. Which one keeps the edge furthest from a hand?

flow.do: Let your child build the cover. Tell them the test: shake the covered blade three times, and then try to touch the edge through the cover with a finger. The edge must stay hidden. Let them improve it and test again.
flow.say: Build your cover. Then shake it three times. Can you still reach the blade? If so, improve it.
flow.kid: Build your cover. Shake it three times. Can your finger touch the card edge? Improve it if so.
flow.parent: Cardboard bends. If the card edge pokes through the cover, add a second layer or fold the cover wider. A cover that works only if you remember is not as good as one that works by its shape.

flow.do: Ask your child to show the cover to another person. They say what is good about it and what could still go wrong.
flow.say: Show your cover. What is good about it? What could still go wrong? Which design in our home does the same job, such as a peeler or school scissors?
flow.kid: Show your cover. What is good about it? What could still go wrong?

ask.q: Does your cover keep you safe if you forget a rule?
good: Yes, because the blade is hidden inside.
Mostly, but I could still touch it from the top.

challenges.context: A good tool is safe even when someone forgets a rule. You design a cover for a pretend blade, as engineers do for real tools.

setup.caption: 2. Build your cover.

challenges.title: A cupboard that cannot be tipped by a small poke
challenges.problem: A tall box is a cupboard. It must hold one heavy bag and two light bags, and it must need a firm push before it falls over.
constraints: The heavy bag, about as heavy as a water bottle, must be inside the box.
Test every design in the same way, with one finger poking the top edge sideways, at touch, tap and firm push.
The box must still stand on its small end. You may add things to it, such as card or tape.
materials: a heavy bag of rice or lentils
two light bags of cotton or paper
a wall or a big book to lean on
general: Put the heavy bag at the bottom. This lowers the balance point.
Widen the base. Tape a flat card under the box, wider than the box.
Fix the cupboard to a wall, with tape or a strap, so it cannot fall forward.
creative: Hang the heavy bag low from a string, so it swings below the box.
Make the bottom round and heavy, like the clay thalaiyatti bommai doll that rocks back up.
Add card legs that stick out sideways, like the legs of a camera tripod.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own way to make the cupboard steady. Test it with touch, tap and firm push. Which design is the hardest to tip? Is there more than one good answer?

flow.do: Stand the box on its small end. Put the heavy bag at the top and the two light bags below. Poke it and see how little it takes to tip.
flow.say: This is a bad cupboard. The heavy bag is on top. Let us poke it and see. How little does it take to tip?
flow.kid: Put the heavy bag at the top. Poke the box. How little does it take to tip?
flow.context: This is the first step of the cupboard challenge. You start with a cupboard that tips easily.

flow.do: Ask your child to write or say three ideas for making the cupboard steadier. Ask which one they think will work best, and why.
flow.say: Think like an engineer. What could we change to make it hard to tip? Say three ideas.
flow.kid: Say three ideas for a steady cupboard. Which will work best?

flow.do: Let your child try one idea at a time. After each, poke the top edge at touch, tap and firm push, and write the level that tipped it. Try the idea of a wider base, the heavy bag at the bottom, and the wall.
flow.say: Try one idea at a time. Poke the same way each time. Write when it falls. Which idea is best?
flow.kid: Try each idea. Poke the same way. Write when it falls.
flow.parent: The heavy bag at the bottom is almost always the biggest change. A wider base helps too. A box taped to a wall will not fall forward at all, which is why real tall cupboards are fixed to walls.

flow.do: Ask your child to say which design was hardest to tip, and to say where heavy things go in a real cupboard.
flow.say: Which design was hardest to tip? Where do heavy things go in a real cupboard? What could you do at home?
flow.kid: Which design was hardest to tip? Where do heavy things go in a real cupboard?

ask.q: What could you change at home after this challenge?
good: Move heavy things to the bottom shelf.
Ask a grown-up to fix the tall cupboard to the wall.

challenges.context: A tall cupboard can fall on a child who climbs the drawers. You design a steady cupboard with a box.

challenges.title: Carry the heavy bag across the room
challenges.problem: Move a bag that weighs as much as two water bottles from one end of a room to the other without straining your back.
constraints: The bag stays the same weight, so you cannot take things out.
You may use things you find at home, but nothing sharp or hot.
Count how many steps you can carry it before your arms ask to stop, for each way.
materials: a bag with about 2 kilograms of rice, lentils or books
a school bag with two straps
a broom handle or a long stick
a rolling pin or round pencils
a friend or a grown-up to share
general: Hug the bag to your chest and stand up with your legs.
Put the load in a school bag and wear it on both shoulders, close to your back.
Split the bag into two smaller bags and carry one in each hand.
creative: Tie the bag in a cloth sling and carry it on your back, like many people carry a baby or a bundle.
Share the load. Hang the bag from a stick that two people carry between them, so each carries half.
Do not lift it at all. Put it on a cloth and slide it, or on round pencils and roll it.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own way. Count the steps each way takes before you are tired. Which is easiest? Is there more than one good answer?

flow.do: Mark a start and a finish about 5 metres apart. Ask your child to carry the bag by hand, away from the body. They count the steps until they want to stop.
flow.say: First, let us carry it the plain way, with arms out. Count your steps until your arms say stop.
flow.kid: Carry the bag with straight arms. Count your steps until you want to stop.
flow.context: This is the first step of the heavy bag challenge. You find out how hard the plain way is.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three ideas for making the carry easier before they try any.
flow.say: Think like an engineer. How could we make it easier to carry? Say three ideas.
flow.kid: Say three ideas for carrying the bag more easily.

flow.do: Let your child try each idea in turn and count the steps. Stop an idea if it hurts. Do the hug, the school bag, the cloth sling, the stick between two people, and the slide.
flow.say: Try each idea one at a time. Count the steps. Which way was the easiest? Which way hurt the least?
flow.kid: Try each idea. Count the steps. Stop if anything hurts.
flow.parent: Sharing is usually the easiest. A school bag on both shoulders sits close to the back, so it is easy. Never let a child lift more than a load that feels easy.

flow.do: Ask your child which way was easiest and why, and when it is better not to lift at all.
flow.say: Which way was easiest? Why? When is it best not to lift at all?
flow.kid: Which way was easiest? When is it best not to lift at all?

ask.q: When is it better not to lift at all?
good: When it is too heavy.
When I can slide or roll it.
When I can share it.

games.title: Alone, With a Grown-Up, or a Grown-Up's Job?

items.f: Peeling a banana
items.b: I CAN DO IT ALONE. Peeling a banana has no sharp, hot or heavy part.

items.f: Carrying an empty steel plate with two hands
items.b: I CAN DO IT ALONE. An empty plate is light and has no edge that cuts.

items.f: Drinking cool water from a steel tumbler
items.b: I CAN DO IT ALONE. Cool water cannot burn, and a tumbler is light.

items.f: Washing your hands at the tap
items.b: I CAN DO IT ALONE. Clean running water is safe and keeps germs away.

items.f: Carrying a one-litre bottle of water close to your chest
items.b: I CAN DO IT ALONE. The bottle weighs about a kilogram. Hold it close.

items.f: Putting toys away on a low shelf
items.b: I CAN DO IT ALONE. Low shelves are the right place for things you use.

items.f: Taking a tomato out of the fridge
items.b: I CAN DO IT ALONE. A tomato is soft, cold and light.

items.f: Cutting a banana with a plastic knife
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. Soft food and a plastic knife are the safest start, with a grown-up close.

items.f: Cutting paper with round-tip school scissors
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. Scissors have two blades. A grown-up watches the fingers and the edge.

items.f: Peeling a potato with a peeler
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. The blade is small but real. A grown-up steadies the potato.

items.f: Stirring cold curd with a wooden spoon
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. A wooden spoon is blunt. The bowl can slide, so a grown-up holds it.

items.f: Washing a steel bowl in the sink
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. A knife can hide in soapy water, so a grown-up checks the sink first.

items.f: Putting a plaster on a tiny scratch
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. A grown-up checks the scratch is clean and small.

items.f: Starting to cool a burn under a running tap
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. Tell a grown-up at once. Start the cool water while they come.

items.f: Carrying a full school bag on both shoulders
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. Close to the back is good. A grown-up checks it is not too heavy.

items.f: Pressing a clean cloth on a small cut
items.b: WITH A GROWN-UP BESIDE ME. Tell a grown-up first. They help with the washing and the plaster.

items.f: Lifting the lid of a pot of boiling dal
items.b: A GROWN-UP'S JOB. Steam burns skin, and boiling dal is much hotter than a burn needs.

items.f: Carrying a cup of hot tea
items.b: A GROWN-UP'S JOB. A spill is a scald. A child's skin is thinner and burns sooner.

items.f: Switching on the gas stove
items.b: A GROWN-UP'S JOB. A flame needs fuel, air and heat. A grown-up controls all three.

items.f: Plugging in a mixer with wet hands
items.b: A GROWN-UP'S JOB. Wet hands carry electricity more easily. A grown-up does the plugging.

items.f: Frying in hot oil
items.b: A GROWN-UP'S JOB. Hot oil is much hotter than boiling water, and it splashes.

items.f: Sharpening a knife on a stone
items.b: A GROWN-UP'S JOB. A freshly sharpened edge is thinner than a hair. This is for grown-ups only.

items.f: Lifting a full bucket of water
items.b: A GROWN-UP'S JOB. A full bucket weighs about fifteen kilograms. That is too much for a child.

items.f: Getting a glass jar down from a high shelf
items.b: A GROWN-UP'S JOB. A jar from a high shelf is heavy and sharp if it breaks. Never climb for it.

rules: Cut out the 24 cards, the three mats and the 20 star tokens. Lay the three mats side by side. Shuffle the cards and put the top 12 in a pile, face down. The rest go back in the box.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud. Put it on the mat you think is right.
Say why in one sentence. Then say one thing that would make it safer. A good reason wins one star.
Turn the card over and read the back. If the back says something different from your mat, you can still keep your star if your reason was good. Two answers can both be worth defending.
When all 12 cards have been played, count the stars together. Your team goal is 10 stars or more.
If two players are playing against each other, the player with more stars wins. If you tie, you both win. Playing alone, try to beat your own score the next day.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three mats on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 24 cards and put the top 12 face down in a pile. 3. Put the 20 star tokens in a bowl.

flow.parent: Some cards can go two ways. Cutting paper with round-tip scissors could be alone in some homes. The back gives the usual answer. A good reason matters more than the mat.

flow.do: Count the stars. Ask your child which card they would put on a different mat, if they could choose again.
flow.say: Count our stars. Which card was hardest to place? Why?
flow.kid: Count the stars. Which card was hardest to place? Why?

worksheets.title: Sharp, hot and heavy: the first steps (core)

items.p: Where does your hand go on a knife or a pair of scissors?
opts: On the handle or the rings
items.why: Your hand belongs on the holding part. Picking the edge means thinking the working part is the safe place to hold. The working part is the part that cuts.

items.p: A thin edge cuts because the whole push lands on a tiny place.
items.why: True. A wide palm spreads the push out. A thin edge puts the whole push on a thin line, so it cuts.

items.p: You press dough with your palm and with a ruler's edge, with the same push. The ____ goes deeper.
items.why: The thin edge touches a smaller place, so the push is bigger there. Picking 'palm' means thinking a bigger part pushes harder.

items.p: Match each tool to its working part.
items.why: The working part does the job. The handle, the rings, the frame and the knob are the parts you hold or touch.

items.p: Sort each one by what makes it a danger.
items.why: Edges are sharp, heat burns and weight falls hard. Some things are two dangers at once, like a glass jar on a high shelf.

items.p: Put the steps of first aid for a small cut in order.
items: Press a clean cloth on the cut
items.why: Tell a grown-up first. Pressing lets the platelets build their plug. Washing carries dirt and germs away. A plaster keeps the cut clean.

items.p: A burn is cooled under running water for about 20 minutes.
items.why: True. A burn keeps burning after you pull away because the heat is still in the skin. Cool water carries it out.

items.p: Why does a ladle have a wooden handle and a steel bowl?
items.a: Steel lets heat move through quickly, and the bowl must be hot to cook. Wood lets heat move slowly, so my hand stays cool.
items.why: Steel is a conductor and wood is an insulator. The working part is steel and the holding part is wood.

items.p: Draw yourself carrying scissors the safe way. Show which way the points face.
items.a: The scissors are closed and held by the rings. The points face down, close to the leg. The child walks and looks ahead.
items.why: Closed scissors held by the rings with the points down keep the edge away from the body and the legs.

items.p: Should a seven-year-old learn to cut with a real knife, with a grown-up beside them?

views.who: A teacher who follows Maria Montessori
views.says: Children can use real tools, if the tools fit their hands and a grown-up is near. Careful practice builds steady hands.

views.who: A doctor who treats children's injuries
views.says: A moment of looking away can hurt a hand for life. A plastic knife gives practice with less risk.

items.ask: Which would you choose for yourself? Say why. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A good answer picks one and gives a reason about risk or learning. It says what the other person has right, such as steady hands or a moment's lapse.
items.why: People who care about children disagree here. Both want a child safe and skilled. Nobody has settled it with a large study.

items.p: Which way of holding a full bottle feels easiest for longest?
opts: Out in front with straight arms
items.why: The bottle weighs the same. The farther a load is from your body, the harder your muscles work.

items.p: Where is the best place for a heavy bag of rice?
opts: On the floor or a low shelf
items.why: Heavy things low cannot fall far and cannot tip a cupboard. A high shelf is where a heavy thing falls hardest.

worksheets.title: Cuts, burns and why things tip (stretch)

items.p: Many cooks say a blunt knife slips off a smooth tomato more easily than a sharp one. What is their reason?
opts: It needs a harder push, so it slides sideways
items.why: A blunt edge is thick, so you push harder. On a slippery skin the hard push can slide the knife sideways. Many cooks say sharp is safer. Nobody has settled it.

items.p: Rust gives you tetanus.
items.why: False. Rust is only iron that has joined with oxygen. Tetanus bacteria live in soil and dung, and a muddy nail carries them.

items.p: Tetanus bacteria live in ____, not in rust.
items.why: Tetanus bacteria wait in soil and dust as spores. A deep, muddy cut with little air suits them.

items.p: Match each thing to what heat does in it.
items.why: Steel is a conductor, so heat moves quickly. Wood and dry cloth are insulators. Wet cloth carries heat, and it can turn to steam.

items.p: Sort each one for a burn: DO or DO NOT.
items: take off bangles near the burn
cover loosely with a clean cloth
items.why: Water takes out the heat. Ice can harm skin again. Toothpaste, butter and ghee hold the heat in and can carry germs.

items.p: Put these in order, from the lightest to the heaviest.
items.why: A pencil weighs a few grams. A full one-litre bottle weighs about one kilogram. A full bucket can weigh about fifteen.

items.p: A pan of burning oil can be put out by pouring water on it.
items.why: False. The water sinks under the oil, turns to steam in an instant and throws burning oil out. A grown-up slides a lid on.

items.p: Your hand jumps from a hot pan before you feel pain. Why is that useful?
items.a: The message goes to the spinal cord, and the spinal cord sends back 'pull away' without waiting for the brain. This saves time, so my hand burns less.
items.why: A reflex is faster than thinking. It only starts after the touch, so it cannot do everything.

items.p: Draw a cupboard with a heavy rice sack, a bag of cotton and a glass jar. Show where each goes.
items.a: The rice sack goes on the bottom shelf. The cotton bag goes on a higher shelf. The glass jar goes low, not on the top.
items.why: Heavy things go low so the cupboard does not tip. A glass jar is heavy and sharp if it breaks, so it also stays low.

items.p: A grandmother puts turmeric on a cut. A nurse says wash it and cover it.

views.who: A grandmother in a family that has used turmeric for generations
views.says: Turmeric has been used for a very long time. Laboratory tests find that it helps skin grow.
Clean water and a clean cover are proven to work. Turmeric powder is not germ-free and can hide a deep cut.

items.ask: Which would you do first? Say why. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A good answer says to wash and cover first, as proven. It also says the lab results for turmeric are promising and that careful trials in people are few.
items.why: The evidence for washing and covering is strong. The evidence for turmeric in people is thin, and science has not settled it.

items.p: Which keeps you safe on a day you forget a rule?
opts: A tool with a guard built in
items.why: Engineers do not rely only on care. A guard or a hidden blade keeps working when a person forgets.

items.p: A bucket weighs 12 kilograms. Two children carry it together. Each carries ____ kilograms.
items.why: 12 shared between 2 is 6 each. 6 + 6 = 12.

items.p: The same push lands on your thumb and on a pin's tip. Where is the pressure bigger?
items.why: The same push on a smaller place is a bigger pressure. The pin's tip is tiny. The thumb is wide.

items.p: A push of 12 over 4 squares is 3 on each. On 1 square the same push is ____.
items.why: 12 divided by 1 is 12. A push on a smaller place is stronger there.

items.p: Blowing on a cut makes it clean.
items.why: False. Blowing or licking a cut puts germs from the mouth on it. Clean running water is better.

items.p: A friend says rust gives tetanus. What do you say, and what would you ask to test it?
items.a: Rust is iron joined with oxygen. Tetanus comes from bacteria in soil, so a muddy nail is the danger, not the rust. I would ask whether a clean rusty spoon in a dry kitchen has ever caused tetanus.
items.why: Testing an idea means asking what else would be true if it were right. Many rusty things are clean and many shiny nails are muddy.

items.p: A glass jar on a high shelf is two dangers. Which two?
opts: Heavy when it falls and sharp when it breaks
items.why: A jar from a high shelf falls with a lot of push, and then its pieces are sharp. Heat is not part of it.

items.p: A pan can be hot enough to burn you with no flame under it.
items.why: True. A pan keeps its heat for a long time after the flame is off, and you cannot see that it is hot.

items.p: A thread cuts dough, but a steel ruler laid flat does not. Why?
items.a: The thread touches the dough along a thin line, so the push lands on a tiny place. The flat ruler touches a wide place, so the same push spreads out.
items.why: Danger comes from the meeting of a push and a small place. A flat steel ruler is hard, but a wide place gives a small pressure.

items.p: Draw a cat's paw with the claws out, and a cat's paw with the claws hidden. Say when she uses each.
items.a: The first paw has curved claws out for climbing or scratching. The second paw is soft and the claws are folded in.
items.why: A cat keeps her claws away until she needs them. People do something like this when we put a blade away in a drawer.

items.p: An engineer says: design the danger out. A grandmother says: be careful and look.

views.who: An engineer who designs kitchen tools
views.says: Careful people still make mistakes. A tool with a guard keeps working on the day you forget.

views.who: A grandmother who has cooked for sixty years
views.says: No guard thinks for you. A cook who looks and listens avoids most trouble.

items.ask: Which matters more? Say why. Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A good answer weighs both. Guards help on the day we forget, and attention helps with everything a guard does not cover. A good answer says both are needed.
items.why: Both are right about something. Engineers add a guard first, then ask what the person must still remember.

items.p: A cupboard with all its heavy things on top is likely to...
opts: tip over with a small pull
items.why: A high balance point means a small tilt moves the weight past the base. Tall cupboards need heavy things low, and a fixing to the wall.

items.p: Put these in order, from the smallest harm to the biggest.
items: a cut finger with a plaster
a cupboard falling on a child
items.why: Think of how likely the harm is and how bad it is. A small cut heals. A boiling-water burn or a falling cupboard can harm for life.

items.p: A person who feels no pain gets many burns. Why does pain help us?
items.a: Pain is an alarm. It tells me where the body is hurt, so I pull away and look after the place. Without it a burn can go on and on without being noticed.
items.why: Pain is useful. Nobody can yet explain why a signal in a nerve feels like hurting. That is an open question.

quiz.p: You press a pencil tip and a fingertip on your hand with the same push. Why does the tip hurt more?
opts: The push lands on a tiny place
quiz.why: The push is the same, but a tiny place gets more of it on each bit of skin. Picking 'pushes harder' mixes up the push with the place it lands on.

quiz.p: A cook wants to cut soft cheese neatly. Which tool is best?
quiz.why: The wire touches a thin line, so the push is large there. A flat plate spreads the push out.

quiz.p: A drawing pin has a wide top and a tiny point. Why?
opts: The wide top is gentle on the thumb
quiz.why: The wide top spreads your push, so the thumb stays safe. The tiny point puts the same push on one spot, so the pin goes into the board.

quiz.p: Someone calls your name while you are holding a tool. What do you do first?
opts: Put the tool down, then look up
Look up and keep holding it
quiz.why: Your hand moves when your eyes move. A tool is put down first, so the edge is not in the way.

quiz.p: A knife slips off the counter. What is the safest thing to do?
opts: Step back and let it fall
quiz.why: A falling knife has no handle in the air. Catching it is how people get cut. Stepping back is safe.

quiz.p: A small cut is bleeding. After you tell a grown-up, what is first?
opts: Press a clean cloth on it
Lift the cloth to peep every minute
quiz.why: Pressing helps the platelets build their plug. Peeping breaks the plug, and blowing puts mouth germs on it.

quiz.p: A deep cut came from a nail that lay in the mud. What next?
quiz.why: A deep, muddy cut can let tetanus bacteria in. A doctor can help. Butter holds germs on the skin.

quiz.p: Why does a steel spoon left in hot dal get a hot handle?
opts: The handle is closer to the flame
quiz.why: Steel is a conductor, so heat travels along it fast. Wood is an insulator, so a wooden spoon stays cool.

quiz.p: Which can burn skin with no flame at all?
quiz.why: Steam carries a lot of heat and gives it out when it turns back to water on skin. This is a scald.

quiz.p: You touch a hot pan. What is the best first help?
opts: Cool running water for about 20 minutes
quiz.why: Cool running water takes the heat out of the skin. Ghee holds the heat in. Ice can harm the skin again.

quiz.p: Which way of lifting a heavy bag is best for your back?
opts: Stand close, bend your knees and stand up
Bend your back with straight legs
quiz.why: Your legs are strong. A load close to the body makes your back work less. Scientists are still testing which way of lifting protects the back best.

quiz.p: Why are tall cupboards fixed to the wall?
opts: A child who climbs can pull one over
quiz.why: A heavy thing high up tips easily. A climbing child can move the weight past the base. A fixing to the wall stops the fall.

quiz.p: Some say a child should use real knives early. Others say wait. What is true?
opts: A big study has proved the early way is best
People who care about children still disagree
quiz.why: Both sides want children safe. Nobody has run a large study to settle it, so we weigh both views.

quiz.p: Some families put turmeric on cuts. What is the fair thing to say?
opts: Lab tests look good, but proof in people is thin
It is proven to be useless
quiz.why: Studies in labs and on animals are promising. Careful trials on people are few. Clean water and a clean cover are proven.

School scissors have rounded tips, so the point cannot stab a finger. Engineers designed the danger out.
Look at the top of a pressure cooker. A small valve lets steam escape if the pressure gets too high, so the cooker does not burst.
A steel ladle has a wooden or plastic handle, because heat moves slowly through wood and plastic.
A cook lifts a hot pot with a thick, dry cloth. A wet cloth would carry the heat to the hand.
Builders fix tall cupboards to the wall and put heavy things low, so a cupboard cannot be pulled over.
Porters at railway stations carry suitcases on the head, right above the backbone, so the load is close to the body.
Look at the three pins of a plug. The longest pin goes into the socket first. It gives stray electricity a safe path to the ground.

maths.problem: A push of 12 lands on a flat ruler that covers 6 squares of paper. The same push lands on the ruler's thin edge, which covers 1 square. How much push is on each square for each?
maths.answer: 2 on each square for the flat ruler. 12 on the one square for the edge.
maths.explain: Share the push over the squares it covers. 12 shared between 6 squares is 2 on each square. 12 on 1 square is 12. The edge gives 6 times as much on its square, because 12 is 6 times 2.
maths.why_maths: Sharing a push over the size of the place it lands on is exactly how scientists find pressure.

maths.problem: You start cooling a burn at 4:10. It needs about 20 minutes of cool running water. At what time can you stop?
maths.explain: 20 minutes after 4:10 is 4:30. 10 more minutes reach 4:20, and 10 more reach 4:30.
maths.why_maths: Reading a clock and adding minutes is how you know the cooling is long enough, because a short cooling does not work.

maths.problem: A bucket weighs 12 kilograms. Two children carry it together, and then three children carry it together. How much does each carry in the two cases?
maths.answer: 6 kilograms each for two children. 4 kilograms each for three children.
maths.explain: Half of 12 is 6, because 6 + 6 = 12. A third of 12 is 4, because 4 + 4 + 4 = 12. More helpers means a smaller share each.
maths.why_maths: Sharing a load into equal parts shows how many hands make a heavy thing easy to carry.

quiz: A thin edge cuts because it puts the whole push on a tiny spot.
A small place gives a bigger pressure, so a thin edge cuts.
Your hand belongs on the working part of a tool.
Your hand goes on the holding part. The working part does the cutting or the heating.
You can cool a burn with ice.
Ice can harm the skin again. Cool running water for about 20 minutes is better.
Rust gives you tetanus.
Tetanus bacteria live in soil. A muddy nail carries them, rusty or not.
Heat moves quickly along steel.
Steel is a conductor, so the handle of a steel spoon in hot dal gets hot.
A heavy thing is safest on a high shelf.
A heavy thing high up falls hard and can tip a cupboard. Heavy things go low.
Steam can burn you even with no flame.
Hot liquid and steam carry heat. That is a scald.
You press a clean cloth on a bleeding cut and do not lift it to peep.
Pressing helps the clot form. Peeping tears it open again.
A load feels easier to hold close to your body.
Held far out, a load makes your arm and shoulder muscles work harder.
Some people and scientists still disagree about when a child should use a real knife.
Both sides want children safe, and nobody has settled it with a large study.
odd: The knife, the peeler and the grater all have a working edge. A pillow does not cut.
Wood, dry cloth and plastic are insulators. Steel lets heat through quickly.
The clot, the scab and the platelets are made by the body. A plaster is put on from outside.
Steam, hot tea and hot oil can all burn. Cold water cools a burn.
A rice sack, a full bucket and a bottle of water are heavy. A feather is very light.
